story.title: Muslims Expected to Surpass Christians as Largest Religion by 2035
story.summary: According to projections from the Pew Research Center, Muslims are expected to outnumber Christians by 2035, with estimates of 2.57 billion Muslims compared to 2.52 billion Christians. This shift is attributed to differences in fertility rates between the two groups. The projections indicate significant changes in the global religious landscape over the coming years.

explore_lenses.label: Why is Islam projected to grow faster?
explore_lenses.title: Births and age structure drive the gap
explore_lenses.summary: Pew attributes the projected crossover chiefly to demographic differences, not to a large flow of converts from Christianity to Islam.

claims.text: Pew estimates that Muslim women had an average total fertility rate of 3.1 children in 2020-2025, compared with 2.5 among Christian women; Muslims also have a comparatively young age profile.
Forecast: Pew projects natural population change to add 1.6 billion Muslims from 2020 to 2070, versus 792 million Christians.

Forecast: Pew estimates that movement between Islam and Christianity will be nearly balanced—9.2 million Muslims becoming Christian and 9 million Christians becoming Muslim—so conversion is not the main explanation for Islam’s projected growth.

explore_lenses.label: Where will the religious landscape shift most?
explore_lenses.title: Sub-Saharan Africa becomes more central
explore_lenses.summary: The global ranking change does not mean either faith becomes dominant everywhere. The largest demographic shifts are projected in sub-Saharan Africa, while Christianity remains numerically large and grows worldwide.

claims.text: Forecast: By 2070, Pew projects 54% of the world’s Christians will live in sub-Saharan Africa, compared with 31% in 2020; the region’s Christian population is projected to rise from 697 million to 1.6 billion.
Forecast: Muslims in sub-Saharan Africa are projected to rise from 369 million to 980 million by 2070, and the region’s share of the world’s Muslims is projected to increase from 18% to 27%.

Forecast: Pew projects Christians will still be the largest religious group in most world regions in 2070; the only regional change in the largest group is projected to be in Asia-Pacific, where Muslims would surpass the religiously unaffiliated.

explore_lenses.label: How certain is a 2035 crossover?
explore_lenses.title: It is a conditional forecast, not a fixed date
explore_lenses.summary: The 2035 estimate follows Pew’s model of recent demographic patterns continuing. Pew’s alternative scenarios show that some inputs, especially switching and migration, can materially affect regional outcomes, though it says the worldwide Muslim-Christian crossover persists even without switching.

claims.text: Forecast: Pew projects 2.57 billion Muslims and 2.52 billion Christians in 2035, with both populations larger than in 2020.

Pew bases the projections on age structure, fertility, mortality, migration and religious switching across 201 countries and territories, assuming that recently observed switching and migration patterns continue.
Forecast: In Pew’s hypothetical no-switching scenario, Muslims still surpass Christians globally because age structure and fertility have a much larger modeled effect than switching.

Forecast: Pew finds migration is especially consequential for regional Muslim shares—for example, Europe’s projected Muslim share in 2070 is 13% in the main scenario but 9% if migration stopped after 2020.

story_report.summary: Pew Research Center projects that Muslims will become the world’s largest religious group by 2035, reaching an estimated 2.57 billion people compared with 2.52 billion Christians. Both communities are projected to grow from their 2020 populations, but the forecast would place Muslims ahead globally. The projected shift is driven chiefly by demographic patterns, particularly higher fertility among Muslims and a younger Muslim age profile, rather than by large-scale religious conversion.

sections.heading: Demographic Forces Behind Muslim Growth
sections.body: Pew estimates that Muslim women had an average total fertility rate of 3.1 children from 2020 to 2025, compared with 2.5 among Christian women. It projects that natural population change will add 1.6 billion Muslims between 2020 and 2070, versus 792 million Christians. Religious switching is expected to have a far smaller effect: Pew estimates 9.2 million Muslims will become Christian and 9 million Christians will become Muslim over that period.

sections.heading: Sub-Saharan Africa Reshapes Religious Distribution
sections.body: Sub-Saharan Africa is projected to account for an increasing share of both major religious populations. Pew forecasts that the region’s Christian population will rise from 697 million in 2020 to 1.6 billion in 2070, when 54% of the world’s Christians would live there, up from 31%. Its Muslim population is projected to grow from 369 million to 980 million, increasing the region’s share of Muslims worldwide from 18% to 27%.

sections.heading: Christianity Remains Regionally Predominant
sections.body: Despite the projected global crossover, Pew forecasts that Christians will remain the largest religious group in most world regions in 2070. The only projected regional change in the largest group is in Asia-Pacific, where Muslims would surpass the religiously unaffiliated. Pew’s projections cover 201 countries and territories and model age structure, fertility, mortality, migration and religious switching, assuming recently observed switching and migration patterns continue.

unresolved.text: The timing and scale of a global Muslim-Christian crossover remain uncertain because fertility, mortality, migration, religious affiliation and switching patterns can change over time; Pew presents demographic projections rather than counts of future believers.

related_stories.title: New Knesset Speaker Elected in Israel, Signaling Shift in Government Dynamics
related_stories.summary: The Israeli parliament has elected Matan Kahana as the new speaker, marking a significant shift in the Knesset following Benjamin Netanyahu's loss of majority. Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot, received 66 votes in the 120-member chamber, indicating a move towards reversing policies from the outgoing government led by Netanyahu.

related_stories.title: Cincinnati Zoo's Fiona the Hippo Receives Care After Hat Ingestion
related_stories.summary: Fiona, a hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo, is receiving fluids and supportive care after swallowing a hat. Zookeepers have stated that she cannot undergo surgery to remove the object and are focusing on helping her pass it naturally.
